A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same rank-statistic f-divergence construction. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic divergence-estimation experiments, particle-transport demonstrations, CelebA samples, and MNIST training comparisons in Section 4 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original estimation and MNIST results and reports additional CIFAR-10 generation, synthetic and image two-sample testing, and time-to-quality experiments.

M1.justification: The central rank/Bernstein estimator and transport constructions remain. Appendix C.5.2 adds generator training with rank-TV in discriminator feature space and a hybrid adversarial-loss variant; C.7 introduces permutation-calibrated testing using the chi-square specialization. Algorithm 1 also drops optional monotone-rank reordering. These are localized procedural extensions.

E1.justification: CIFAR-10 replaces CelebA for image transport, and CIFAR-10-C adds realistic corruption-detection coverage. New experiments cover two-sample hypothesis testing, copula dependence alternatives, and generation of two-moons distributions with higher-dimensional extensions. The earlier estimation families, four transport toys, and MNIST remain.

E2.justification: The neural-KL and MNIST comparator sets are retained. New reported comparisons include Hotelling's T2, sliced optimal transport, MMD, and tuned MMD in Figures 12–13; C2ST in Figure 14; and sliced Wasserstein, MMD, and full assignment OT for generator training in Table 6.

E3.justification: New testing protocols include permutation calibration, with Figure 11 specifying N=M=2000, K=4, L=64, and 500 permutations. Appendix E adds shared-generator comparisons with external classifier-JS stopping criteria and a 3000-step budget. CO-RPT's rank schedule changes alongside the dataset replacement. Appendix C.1 corrects its random-projection description to coordinate-axis summation, matching v1's main text; this does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds null-calibration checks, power-versus-runtime analyses across scale, shape, and dependence alternatives, and corruption-severity/sample-size analyses on CIFAR-10-C. Appendix E adds computational-cost and time-to-quality analyses. The earlier resolution, tail-behavior, and dimensionality analyses remain.

E5.justification: Existing 10-run mean-and-standard-deviation reporting is retained. New testing figures add rejection-rate standard errors over 100 repetitions and 95% binomial confidence intervals; Figure 14 specifies 10 independent C2ST trials per corruption–severity pair. These are additional reporting practices for new experiments, not increased run counts for retained benchmarks.

E6.justification: The numerical contents of v1 Tables 1–4 match v2 Tables 1, 3, 4, and 5. Newly reported outcomes include testing power and calibration, CIFAR-10 feature-training FID decreasing from roughly 380 to 41, and Table 6 timing results: at d=4, Rank takes 131.6 seconds versus SWD's 117.6. CelebA samples are replaced by CIFAR-10 samples; these are different-setting results.

T1.justification: v2 introduces atomless-reference assumptions and revises Theorem 3.3 to require Lipschitz f', allow zero limiting variance, and provide a positivity criterion. New Theorem 3.4 and Appendix B.9 establish oracle-reference asymptotic normality for growing resolution, with sqrt(N) << K_N << N under smoothness assumptions. Several existing proof terms and constants are also corrected.

C1.justification: The abstract and four principal contributions retain the same scientific claims: optimization-free rank approximation, monotonicity and lower bounds, convergence and sampling guarantees, slicing, and usefulness for generative learning. More specific transport/pretraining wording and additional evidence do not materially redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds practical interpretation of K's approximation–sampling tradeoff and L's projection error. Table 1 explains empirical ratios above one, and C.5.2 qualifies feature-space discrepancies as representation-dependent. New discussions qualify efficiency by setting and acknowledge unfavorable dependence alternatives. Most of the existing limitations discussion is retained.

D1.justification: v2 documents logistic soft-CDF comparisons, interpolated quantiles, feature-space training components, testing settings, and generator/classifier architectures and optimization details. Appendix E distinguishes hard- and soft-rank runtime and memory costs. The anonymous code-and-data repository disclosure is replaced by a named GitHub code link; hardware information is unchanged.

R1.justification: Targeted references are added for calibration, goodness-of-fit and two-sample testing, CIFAR benchmarks, and precision–recall divergences. Appendix C.6 newly distinguishes scalar PR-divergence approximation from direct PR-curve estimation. CelebA and some gradient-flow references disappear, while the central positioning as a generalization of earlier rank-based work remains.

P1.justification: v2 clarifies empirical versus population notation, rewrites portions of the estimator and transport explanations, merges the concentration proposition into Theorem 2.6, subdivides the image appendix, and adds an impact statement. Affiliations and contribution notes change. Most existing prose and the overall narrative organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column presentation, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. v2 adds a notation table, a timing table, and Figures 11–16, replaces the Figure 5 image grid, and redisplays the transport snapshots. Existing numerical tables are retained and partly renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens theoretical validity through explicit atomlessness and revised normality conditions, adds a proved resolution-selection result, and resolves the KL benchmark's conflicting protocol descriptions. Calibrated testing and external time-to-quality comparisons provide useful independent validation, including unfavorable cases. The new FID and timing results have limited repeated-run uncertainty reporting, and replacing CelebA is not a same-task performance gain, but these limitations do not outweigh the improvements in rigor and empirical support.
